extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, math students, and problem-solvers writing or evaluating proofs (e.g., Math StackExchange users)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing and recognising 'just-do-it' style constructive proofs: build a sequence a1,a2,… where each inductive step is straightforward because the search space leaves ample wiggle room. Advice also covers when this method fails and stylistic implications for proof-writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core characteristic: sequential constructive proof
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'just-do-it' proof builds a sequence a₁, a₂, … satisfying constraints P₁, P₂, …, where at each stage 'it is not hard to prove that there exists a_{n+1}' satisfying the next constraint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the defining property: reduce the problem to a countable sequence of single requirements and show existence at each step by a straightforward argument. Emphasises explicit construction and stepwise verification rather than simultaneous specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constraints reformulable as a countable sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: Constraints can be reformulated as a countable sequence; each step is a single requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When you can enumerate the constraints P₁,P₂,… the problem is amenable to the just-do-it approach. A key heuristic is to recast a global goal into a sequence of local tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Each inductive step avoids only finitely many obstacles
rubrics_metrics.description: Each inductive step avoids only finitely many obstacles (so the next choice only needs to avoid a finite set).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The existence proof for a_{n+1} should fail only for finitely many candidates, leaving infinitely many (or a large continuous set of) acceptable choices. If each step eliminates only finitely many options, a simple counting or cardinality argument often suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search space vastly exceeds restrictions (ample wiggle room)
rubrics_metrics.description: The search space (e.g. an open disc, an uncountable set) is much larger than the set of restrictions, so wiggle room is always available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer contexts where there is abundant freedom to modify choices; typical justifications invoke cardinality/measure/topology to show that forbidden choices are negligible compared to allowed ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method fails when constraints are global/algebraically coupled
rubrics_metrics.description: The method fails when 'constraints are just too global'—algebraic or global constraints couple the choices and prevent the inductive freedom required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: constructing Hadamard matrices, where algebraic constraints couple entries across the whole object. If making a local choice affects many future constraints in an intertwined algebraic way, a just-do-it induction is unlikely to work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer sequential construction over simultaneous specification
rubrics_metrics.description: When possible, prefer sequential construction to simultaneously specifying the whole object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequential construction often exposes the simple inductive step; simultaneous definitions hide the local choices and can obscure simple existence arguments. This is a stylistic criterion for writing clearer, more elementary proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer explicit procedures over implicit descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer explicit procedures (constructive algorithms) over implicit descriptions when the problem admits it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit procedures make the stepwise argument and the availability of wiggle room transparent; they enhance accessibility and reduce the need for sophisticated ingenuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reformulate problems to expose countability
rubrics_metrics.description: Reformulate problems to expose countability so they can be tackled one constraint at a time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for ways to enumerate requirements (e.g., by listing rational radii/points) so you can apply a simple inductive construction. This is a practical strategy to convert a global requirement into a sequence of local tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use straightforward induction to show feasibility at each stage
rubrics_metrics.description: Use straightforward induction to prove the feasibility of each step in the construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inductive argument should be simple: given a₁,…,a_n satisfying P₁,…,P_n, show existence of a_{n+1} by demonstrating that only a manageable (often finite) set of choices are excluded. Avoid heavy machinery when elementary induction suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise and label the 'just-do-it' pattern; conserve ingenuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognise when the just-do-it pattern applies and reserve ingenuity for genuinely global problems. 'Elementary thinking' and procedural transparency are aesthetic virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly identifying the pattern helps choose an appropriate proof strategy and justifies avoiding overcomplicated arguments. Treat accessibility and procedural transparency as positive goals when the method applies.
